name: A Governance Structure for AI
title: A Governance Structure for AI
answer: A governance structure for AI is a standing committee that maintains a district's published AI rules, reviews tools, and oversees pilots. It matters because rules that nobody maintains, and decisions that nobody publishes, cannot guide which tools a school actually adopts. The committee works best when it holds real authority, meets on a regular schedule, and seats skeptics alongside enthusiasts.

sections.body: Published rules need someone to keep them current, and this idea names that someone as a committee rather than a single person. The committee typically brings together teachers, principals, technology and privacy staff, special education and English learner specialists, and parents, and it reviews tools, updates the rules, and watches over pilots. The problem it solves is drift: a district can write a strong AI policy and then have no body responsible for applying it as new tools arrive. Without clear authority and a regular rhythm, the written rules stop matching what classrooms actually use. The structure also gives the district one place where approval decisions are made and explained.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice the committee runs on a schedule and a published record. A common pattern is monthly meetings to review requests for new tools and quarterly meetings to look at how pilots are going, with decisions posted so staff, families, and students can see which tools are approved and why. Membership is deliberately balanced, with skeptics seated alongside enthusiasts so that questions about privacy, equity, and evidence get asked before approval rather than after. Students can serve on the committee too, and the text points to the high school level as the place where that fits most naturally. The committee also acts when something goes wrong, pulling a tool that did not work in its pilot, that no longer has a privacy agreement behind it, or that has harmed students.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text offers no study, figure, or formal evidence label for this idea, so it rests on practice rather than research. What it gives instead is a set of practical observations about how committees behave: one that meets rarely or keeps its decisions private cannot guide adoption, and one made up only of enthusiasts risks approving tools too quickly. The claim that balanced membership produces better decisions and more trust is presented as the book's own reasoning, not as a finding from a named study. Readers should treat the structure as a workable operating pattern rather than a proven intervention.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits here are about authority and follow through. A committee without clear authority, or one that meets only occasionally, becomes a formality that cannot steer adoption. Keeping decisions private has the same effect, because staff and families cannot tell which tools are approved or on what grounds. The text also warns against a committee of enthusiasts only, since that group may approve tools too quickly and skip hard questions about privacy, equity, and evidence. Governance also means knowing when to stop, so a tool that did not succeed in its pilot, that lost the agreement covering privacy, or that caused harm to students should be pulled quickly, using the exit criteria the book set out earlier.
